source: Kim et al. (2025/2026) InvThink: Premortem Reasoning for Safer Language Models
finding: InvThink makes the model list harms, analyse them, and set mitigation constraints before it answers. It is the first LLM method that calls itself a premortem. As a prompt only, it beat zero-shot, CoT, ToT and a plain safety instruction on professional-ethics harm.
numbers: TRIDENT harmfulness (1-5, lower better), mean over models: zero-shot 3.22, SafetyPrompt 2.62, InvThink prompt 2.19 (32.0% lower than zero-shot). 2,652 prompts, 5 decoding seeds. SafetyBench gain about 5-13%.
quote: merely instructing models to "be safe" is insufficient; they need structured frameworks for identifying and avoiding specific failure modes
limits: Safety task, not general problem solving. Judges include Gemini-2.5 Pro, which was also the teacher for the training variant. Static benchmarks only.
agent_relevance: Evidence that a failure-first step beats a generic 'be careful' instruction at similar token cost. The target is harm, not task accuracy.

source: Kim et al. (2025/2026) InvThink: Premortem Reasoning for Safer Language Models
finding: In agentic insider-threat scenarios (Anthropic's agentic misalignment setup) the prompt-only version cut harmful actions. The fine-tuned version reached zero observed harmful actions.
numbers: Prompt-only InvThink: blackmail rate down 90% and murder-attempt rate down 44% on average. SFT+RL: 0 harmful actions in 100 trials per seed, 5 seeds (Clopper-Pearson upper 95% bound 0.030). Effect largest for reasoning models, which had higher baseline harm.
limits: Zero observed is not zero risk. Simulated scenarios. Did not test an attacker who injects a malicious failure trace.
agent_relevance: Failure imagination helps most where harm depends on downstream consequences, not surface patterns. Matches the idea of a pre-action check for risky actions.

source: Kim et al. (2025/2026) InvThink: Premortem Reasoning for Safer Language Models
finding: The gain depends on the task. Large on open-ended consequence reasoning, small on pattern matching. Category gains on SafetyBench show this.
numbers: SafetyBench accuracy gains: Illegal Activities +15.8% (N=1,767), Physical Health +12.5% (N=1,140), Ethics +10.0% (N=1,926), Mental Health +7.9% (N=1,561), Offensiveness +2.4% (N=1,801). Domain gains over SafetyPrompt on TRIDENT: finance about 11%, law about 8%, medicine about 7%.
limits: Gains are reported against the paper's own baselines.
agent_relevance: Signal-triggered use (G1): run the check when the step has consequences, skip it for simple pattern tasks.

source: Kim et al. (2025/2026) InvThink: Premortem Reasoning for Safer Language Models
finding: Controlled test of direction: the same SFT with positive-goal lists (PROTHINK) instead of harm lists gave the same safety. So the benefit may come from structure and tokens, not from imagining failure.
numbers: Qwen-2.5-7B, 23,063 matched training targets. Both reach safety rate 1.000 on TRIDENT (harmfulness 1.23 InvThink vs 1.01 PROTHINK), StrongREJECT ASR 0.000, XSTest FRR 0.980 for both.
quote: trace direction does not differentiate safety behavior at the SFT stage
limits: Only the SFT stage on refusal-only data, which collapses both to refusal. Authors say direction at the GRPO stage is untested. Prompt-level direction effect is not isolated.
agent_relevance: Key caution: 'imagine failure' may not be special. A matched 'imagine success' control is needed before we credit prospective hindsight itself.

source: Kim et al. (2025/2026) InvThink: Premortem Reasoning for Safer Language Models
finding: Claim of no safety tax: reasoning scores held or rose after InvThink training. Authors link this to a constraint-checking habit.
numbers: Up to +5.0% on GPQA and MATH500, +2.0% on MMLU for SFT+RL; Qwen-3-8B utility study.
limits: Single seed for these numbers, so authors call them suggestive. Training-based, not scaffold only.
agent_relevance: Weak hint that listing what can go wrong helps constraint checking in reasoning. Needs replication on prompt-only use.

source: Kim et al. (2025/2026) InvThink: Premortem Reasoning for Safer Language Models
finding: Scaling: failure-first prompting kept the top safety score at nearly every model size from 0.27B to 72B. CoT safety fell beyond 14B.
numbers: TRIDENT safety-vs-log-size slope on Gemma-3: InvThink 9.0 vs SafetyPrompt 4.9. Qwen-2.5: 4.7 vs 5.8. Qwen-3: 4.0 vs 4.4 (so SafetyPrompt had a steeper slope there; InvThink is a level shift).
limits: Slope advantage holds in one family only.
agent_relevance: Larger models may have more latent knowledge of failure modes that a premortem step surfaces.

source: Liptay et al. (2026) Evaluating Strategic Reasoning in Forecasting Agents (Bench to the Future 2)
finding: Best-known LLM test linking premortem-style content to accuracy. A forecasting agent that beat every frontier agent wrote far more pre/post-mortem analysis (reasons the forecast could be wrong) in its rationales.
numbers: Share of rationales with Pre/Post-mortem in top 3 of 10 CHAMPS KNOW dimensions: SOTA agent 37.8% vs Opus 4.6 about 12%, Gemini 3.1 Pro and GPT-5.4 about 1-10% (table text partly garbled in extraction). SOTA Brier 0.119 vs Opus 4.6 0.130 (delta 0.011, CI 0.006-0.017), Gemini 0.141, GPT-5.4 0.152. N=1,367 questions.
quote: the better forecaster differs primarily in its pre-mortem analysis of its blind spots and consideration of black swans
limits: Correlational. The SOTA agent had a built-in rationale structure and several other changes (ensembling, recalibration, related forecasts). Ranking done by one Gemini 3.1 Pro call on final rationales only. Authors say prompting for a factor does not ensure the agent does it. May overfit BTF-2.
agent_relevance: Premortem-like content tracks accuracy but is confounded with the whole pipeline. No ablation yet. Treat as a hypothesis, not proof.

source: Liptay et al. (2026) Evaluating Strategic Reasoning in Forecasting Agents (Bench to the Future 2)
finding: Biggest differences between the SOTA agent and frontier agents were Pre/Post-mortem, Other perspectives and Wildcards. Authors call all three epistemic: awareness of the limits of one's knowledge.
numbers: Other dimensions top-3 for SOTA agent: Norms 63.1%, Know power players 43.2%, Comparison classes 38.9%, Select right questions 28.1%, Math 22.6%, Other perspectives 20.3%, Adjust and update 5.1%, Wildcards 2.9%. Tetlock's training of humans on these principles gave 6-12% accuracy gains (cited, randomized trial).
limits: Human experts said Hunt-for-info and Adjust-and-update comparisons were not fair and removed them.
agent_relevance: Premortem is one of ten forecasting habits. Our schema might bundle it with outside view and wildcards rather than treat it alone.

source: Liptay et al. (2026) Evaluating Strategic Reasoning in Forecasting Agents (Bench to the Future 2)
finding: Expert human forecasters reviewed 130 worst questions of the plain Opus 4.6 agent. The main failures were not missing premortems but wrong models of actors: leaders' incentives, follow-through, institutional processes.
numbers: 130 questions (worst 5% by accuracy plus worst 5% vs SOTA agent); only cases where a rerun made the same error were kept. Forecast consistency: on 200 hard questions, 45% had 0 of 8 rollouts on the right side of 50%, 18% had all 8.
limits: Question set leans to geopolitics and policy, which may inflate incentive-modeling failures.
agent_relevance: A failure story only helps if the model can generate the true causes. Premortem quality is bounded by world modeling.

source: Liptay et al. (2026) Evaluating Strategic Reasoning in Forecasting Agents (Bench to the Future 2)
finding: Agents differ in cost and accuracy; the better forecaster costs about 3x more per question, so extra reasoning and checks have a price.
numbers: Cost per question: SOTA $1.68, Opus 4.6 $0.55, Gemini 3.1 Pro $0.30, GPT-5.4 $0.24. Mean of 4 agents Brier 0.125.
limits: Cost includes searches and page reads.
agent_relevance: Budget check for G1: a signal-triggered premortem avoids paying this on every step.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Devil's Advocate: Anticipatory Reflection for LLM Agents
finding: Closest premortem use inside an LLM agent loop. Before each action the agent asks what could go wrong with it and writes a backup action, then backtracks to it if the action fails. Zero-shot, GPT-4 on WebArena.
numbers: Success rate after 7 episodes: anticipatory reflection 23.5%, LATS 22.7%, Plan+Act with post-failure reflection 19.8%. Plan revisions per task 0.64 vs LATS 1.16 vs Plan+Act 2.03 (about 45% fewer than LATS as claimed). Actions in first trial 6.39 vs 4.01 for Plan+Act.
quote: What if the picture frame is not in order #179?
limits: No ablation that removes only the anticipatory step. Gap to LATS is 0.8 points on a small benchmark with temperature 1.0 and manual correction of URL-match scoring. Text observations only.
agent_relevance: Direct template: failure question and backup before the action, applied per step. Gain is small and not isolated.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Devil's Advocate: Anticipatory Reflection for LLM Agents
finding: Authors say plain sampling in LATS gave homogeneous actions and an inconsistent curve, while the devil's-advocate question widened the options considered.
numbers: LATS success rate dropped at round 5 of the learning curve. Error analysis: agent takes only partial lessons from past failures (e.g. repeats typing into fields that do not exist).
limits: Explanation is the authors' reading, not tested.
agent_relevance: Anticipation can add diversity of options; it cannot fix a weak model that repeats past errors.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Boundary condition for any 'imagine and critique your own answer' step. Without outside feedback, self-critique lowered accuracy on reasoning tasks. With oracle labels it looked good, which is not real use.
numbers: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 75.1 (round 1) to 74.7 (round 2); CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 to 41.8; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0. With oracle labels GPT-3.5 GSM8K 95.5, GPT-4 97.5. GPT-3.5 kept its answer 74.7% of the time on GSM8K; changes went correct to wrong more than wrong to correct.
quote: LLMs cannot properly judge the correctness of their reasoning
limits: Tests post-hoc critique of an answer, not pre-action failure imagination. Prompts from source papers plus several variants.
agent_relevance: A premortem inside the model has the same weakness: it cannot reliably tell if it is wrong. Prefer external signals (tests, tools, a second source) to trigger and score it (G1).

source: Chen et al. (2025) Reverse Thinking Makes LLMs Stronger Reasoners (RevThink)
finding: Related inversion idea: train a model to make a backward question and reason back from the answer. A form of reasoning from the end state. Trained on teacher data, not prompt-only.
numbers: Average +13.53% over student zero-shot across 12 datasets, +6.84% over best distillation baseline, +6.69% for plain forward distillation. Gemma-7B-Instruct 8-dataset average 46.80 zero-shot to 61.17; Mistral-7B 63.23. Uses 10% of the data to beat SFT on 10x more.
limits: Needs a teacher and fine-tuning. Backward reasoning is about verifying a solution, not imagining failure. Without teacher verification step scores dropped (e.g. StrategyQA 70.97 to 68.63).
agent_relevance: Supports the broader idea that working backward from the end state catches errors, but only as training; not shown as a scaffold.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
finding: Post-mortem counterpart to the premortem: after a failed trial, the agent writes a verbal reflection and keeps it in memory for the next try.
numbers: HumanEval pass@1 91% vs GPT-4 80%; AlfWorld +22% in 12 steps, HotPotQA +20%. Self-reflection gave +8% absolute over episodic memory alone.
quote: Reflexion agents verbally reflect on task feedback signals
limits: Needs trial feedback (tests, environment reward). Relies on repeated attempts, which a premortem tries to avoid.
agent_relevance: Post-mortem works when there is a retry and a feedback signal; a premortem is the option when one try is all we get.

source: Ke et al. (2024) Enhancing Diagnostic Accuracy through Multi-Agent Conversations
finding: A GPT-4 role-play with a devil's advocate agent to cut anchoring and confirmation bias in cases that had been misdiagnosed.
numbers: 16 case reports, 80 simulated runs. Initial diagnosis correct 0/80; after discussion the top differential was correct 57/80 (71.3%), top two 64/80 (80.0%).
limits: No control arm without the devil's advocate. Initial diagnosis was defined by selection to be wrong. Published cases (possible training-data exposure). Text only.
agent_relevance: Shows the role pattern but not that the devil's advocate caused the gain.

source: Lee et al. (2025) Conversational Agents as Catalysts for Critical Thinking (CHI EA)
finding: LLM devil's advocate in human groups raised satisfaction but did not significantly change psychological safety, and added load.
numbers: 48 participants, 12 groups of four. Psychological safety 5.38 to 5.65, not significant (p=0.490). Satisfaction rose significantly; cognitive workload rose slightly.
limits: Small, late-breaking CHI abstract. Satisfaction is not decision quality.
agent_relevance: Adjacent, not a premortem. Shows counterargument tools can add cost without clear accuracy benefit.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) Prospective Hindsight: Self-Calibrating Reinforcement Learning via Prediction-Reality Gaps
finding: Uses the name 'prospective hindsight' but is a training method: reweight rollouts by the gap between what the agent predicted before acting and what happened. Not the Mitchell technique.
numbers: Science Q&A late-training overconfident-failure rate 34.2% (SDPO) to 20.9%; random reweighting left it at 33.3%. Trajectory teacher-score gains +7.2 (RL), +15.3 (OPD), +3.9 (combined). Prospective accuracy up to 87.8%.
quote: the agent's belief at action time invisible to the gradient
limits: At high weight (2.0) the predictor collapses to a near-constant output: OFR 2.5% but a degraded self-model. Needs training.
agent_relevance: Shows that predicting your own outcome before acting is a usable signal, and where it breaks. Name overlap only.

source: Loweimi et al. (2026) A Tutorial on Prompt Engineering: From Messy Thoughts to AI Workflows
finding: Practitioner tutorial gives a premortem prompt recipe: assume the plan has failed, tell the failure story and early warnings, name the most likely failure, the most dangerous failure, the biggest hidden assumption, and a revised plan. Says do steelman first.
numbers: No measured results. Cites Klein's 2007 HBR article.
quote: a premortem changes the question. Instead of asking "Is this a good plan?", the prompt assumes that the plan has failed
limits: Advice only. No test of the order claim ('a failure story told about a weakened plan finds faults the plan does not have').
agent_relevance: A ready output structure for our operator: likely failure, worst failure, hidden assumption, revision.

source: Loweimi et al. (2026) A Tutorial on Prompt Engineering
finding: Frames premortem as one part of a prompt loop with verify-and-escalate stages and machine-readable output fields, for agent loops where another program reads the answer.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Design guidance only.
agent_relevance: Output of a premortem in our agent should be structured fields, not prose.

source: Uniqueness Bias: Why It Matters, How to Curb It (2024)
finding: Human project data. Names premortems with reference-class forecasting as 'decision hygiene' against thinking a project is unique. Does not test premortem.
numbers: Link between uniqueness bias and weaker performance across 219 projects (per arXiv abstract). Premortem cited only as a remedy (Klein 2007).
limits: No premortem experiment; proposal only.
agent_relevance: Confirms again that machine-era papers repeat the premortem advice without measuring it.

source: Search of arXiv for 'premortem' and 'pre-mortem' (this session, 2026-11)
finding: Gap finding. Searching arXiv titles/abstracts found only 3 papers that use premortem as a reasoning method (InvThink, BTF-2, the prompt tutorial). No paper found that tests Mitchell-style prospective hindsight (imagine the outcome has happened) as a prompt against a no-premortem control on task accuracy.
numbers: Hits: premortem search 5 results (1 medical, 2 AI-afterlife ethics, 2 relevant); 'pre-mortem' 4 results (1 relevant). 'prospective hindsight' 2 results (1 RL training paper).
limits: arXiv only; Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex and the arXiv API were rate-limited; WebSearch budget was used up. Other venues (ACL Anthology, SSRN, HCI) not checked.
agent_relevance: The effectiveness evidence for the premortem in LLMs is thin. Our design should include its own ablation, with a matched 'imagine success' control.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Same paper, multi-agent debate result: debate underperforms simple majority-vote self-consistency with the same number of responses. Critique roles may act as extra sampling, not extra thought.
numbers: Full GSM8K test set used instead of the original 100 examples; authors say debate gain is self-consistency, not self-correction.
limits: Details of debate numbers not extracted here beyond this claim.
agent_relevance: Fair comparison for a premortem: give the control arm the same token budget or same number of samples.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Devil's Advocate: Anticipatory Reflection for LLM Agents
finding: The method has three layers: anticipate before acting, check alignment after acting and backtrack, then review the whole plan after completion. So the premortem part is one of three introspection steps.
numbers: Reported total gain over the best zero-shot baseline: 3.5 points. Efficiency: 45% fewer plan revisions.
limits: The gain cannot be split across the three layers.
agent_relevance: If we copy this, add an arm that turns off only the anticipation step.

source: Liptay et al. (2026) Evaluating Strategic Reasoning in Forecasting Agents (Bench to the Future 2)
finding: Frontier agents with a plain prompt differ in measured calibration and refinement, which helps explain what a pre/post-mortem might fix: calibration, not search.
numbers: Calibration (lower better): SOTA 0.002, Opus 4.6 0.005, GPT-5.4 0.010, Gemini 3.1 Pro 0.012. Refinement (higher better): SOTA 0.081, Opus 0.075, Gemini 0.069, GPT-5.4 0.056.
limits: Not a premortem experiment.
agent_relevance: A premortem might act mainly through calibration (shrinking overconfidence); measure that, not just accuracy.
